newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan marshals might against costly hog epidemic.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan marshals might against costly hog epidemic.

text.p: Taiwan intensified its war on a killer hog epidemic on Tuesday, pooling a billion-dollar fund to finance an island-wide slaughter and vaccination drive as economists warned of huge economic setbacks.

The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease has sparked a total ban on pork exports and an army-led eradication campaign that has battered the stock market and promised thousands of layoffs and a new setback for Taiwan's gathering economic recovery.
Economists said the damage could exceed the expectations of central bank chief Sheu Yuan-dong, who said on Monday the crisis could shave a half a percentage point from 1997 growth.
That would erase a hard-won fourth quarter 1996 acceleration that pushed gross domestic product growth above six percent for the first time in several quarters.

ChinaTrust Commercial Bank chief economist Daniel Chen said damage to the huge pork sector, feed and food processors and all related enterprises could reach one percent of GDP -- a staggering T$65.2 billion (US$2.37 billion) in 1996 terms.
State statistics official Chan Teh-sung has said that with some 10 million hogs on the hoof, the pork industry's 1996 export value alone was T$43.6 billion (US$1.55 billion).
The herd size was falling precipitously after the cabinet's Council of Agriculture ordered the slaughter of all hogs -- even healthy ones -- at all affected farms to eradicate the scourge.
With 357 farms confirmed to date, up from just nine on March 20, officials said that so far 389,171 hogs would be destroyed.
Across Taiwan, masked soldiers in plastic suits were using electric prods to stun pigs, then earth movers to move them into incinerators or giant pits.
Even the Taipei Zoo was taking no chances, ordering a 12-day shutdown to isolate its animals from the virus.

Amplifying President Lee Teng-hui's weekend pledge of T$10 billion (US$364 million) in emergency credit, Premier Lien Chan said Taipei was offering T$20 billion in low-interest loans to pig farmers to help them weather the massive slaughter.

Council officials nonetheless cautioned that pork exports would need years to recover, particularly in terms of access to Japan -- which took 99 percent of Taiwan's 1996 pork exports. Japan and South Korea banned imports from Taiwan on March 21.
Pork accounted for 11.3 percent of Taiwan's US$13.67 billion in total 1996 exports to Japan, officials said.
"It will be difficult to resume pork exports to Japan within five years," Chyr Shuang-ching, a senior council official, told Reuters by telephone.
With pork prices rising in Japan, North American exporters were moving to fill the gap, prompting U.S. pork values to rise and packers to boost supplies to meet expected export demand.
Taiwan farm council officials were scrambling to import some US$200 million worth of emergency vaccines -- eight million doses in all -- to combat the fast-spreading epidemic.
Taiwan had only 50,000 doses on hand when the outbreak was confirmed on March 20.
Humans cannot contract the disease but officials were concerned about its possible spread to other livestock, particularly Taiwan's large herd of dairy cows.
Officials said new hog cases would spring up in coming years as vaccination could not eradicate the virus, but merely reduce the infection rate.
"The virus will stay in Taiwan even after we applied vaccine to pigs," one farm council official said. "The vaccine won't kill the virus."
Once controlled and isolated, the virus would die out, he added.
